title: Him, Her, Them: Object Pronouns
description: Glue 'me, him, her, us, them' onto verbs and prepositions — the full Ṣanʿāni set, including the -ish for 'you' to a woman — through the verbs of giving, telling, sending and asking.
approach: GPA Phase 4 — the learner hears requests with object suffixes in a family errand scene, drills the paradigm by ear, then gives and relays instructions.
unlock_condition: Produce eight commands with a correct object suffix on a verb or on لـ, including one to a woman with -ish
can_do: Say 'tell him', 'give it to me', 'with them'

grammar.title: One set of endings for verbs and prepositions
grammar.explanation: The endings you learned for 'my, your, his' on nouns do the same job on verbs and prepositions, with one change: 'me' is -ni on a verb (شافني 'he saw me') but -i on a preposition (لي 'to me', معي 'with me'). The rest is the same everywhere: -ak 'you (m)', -ish 'you (f)' — the Sanaa form; Aden says -ik — -uh 'him / it', -ha 'her', -na 'us', -kum 'you all', -hum 'them'. So: خبّرني، خبّره، خبّرها، خبّرنا، خبّرهم and لي، لك، لش، له، لها، لنا، لكم، لهم. The verbs 'give', 'tell' and 'show' take the person straight on the verb — أدّيني 'give me' — and the thing follows; with 'send' and 'say', the person goes on لـ: أرسل لي، قل له. مع stretches to معا- before most endings: معاه، معاها، معاهم — but معي and معش stay short.

examples.english: Tell him I'm coming in the afternoon
Show me the photo you took (to a woman)

examples.arabic: ما شفتش بيتش من زمان يا فاطمة
examples.transliteration: maa shuftsh baytish min zamaan ya faaṭima
examples.english: I haven't seen your house in ages, Fatima

culture.title: Talking about people who are not in the room
culture.note: Yemeni conversation is full of third parties — the neighbour, the cousin abroad, the landlord — and there are rules for it. Wish them well before you mention them: الله يحفظه 'God keep him', and never leave a name hanging in criticism without a softener like الله يهديه 'God guide him'. Messages travel through people: سلّم لي عليه 'greet him for me' is said at the end of every visit and is really an instruction, so pass it on. Gossip is tolerated when it is about what someone did, not about their family's honour, and the moment someone says خلّيه 'leave him be' the subject closes. To ask about someone's wife, ask about the family: كيف الأهل؟

phrases.english: Give my greetings to your mother and father
God keep him, he helped us a lot
Leave him be, it's none of our business

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'him' ending -uh, shown here on لـ: له 'to him'. On a verb it is the same: شافه 'he saw him', خبّره 'tell him'. Written ـه, often heard as -a after a consonant in Sanaa.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man handing an envelope to another man, arrow pointing at the receiver.
vocabulary.video_hint: Relayed instructions in family scenes; قل له / خبّره.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'her' ending -ha. On a verb: شافها 'he saw her', أرسل لها 'send to her'. Also 'it' for feminine things: خذها 'take it'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman receiving a gift bag from another woman.

example.english: Send her the photo on WhatsApp

vocabulary.video_hint: Any message relayed to a woman; لها / خبّرها.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'them' ending -hum: شافهم، معاهم، عليهم. Old Sanaa also keeps a feminine plural -hin for a group of women.
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy carrying a tray of tea glasses to a group of guests.

example.english: Take the tea to them in the mafraj

vocabulary.video_hint: Hosting scenes; لهم / عليهم when guests are served.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'Me' is -ni on a verb: شافني 'he saw me', خبّرني 'tell me', ساعدني 'help me'. On a preposition it is just -i: لي، معي، عني. Do not say -ni on لـ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman pointing at herself, another woman handing her a phone.

example.english: Tell me what he said to you

vocabulary.video_hint: Requests addressed to camera or a friend; خبّرني / ساعدني.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The 'us' ending -na: شافنا، معانا، أرسل لنا. Same letters as 'our' on a noun (بيتنا), so you already know it.
vocabulary.image_scene: A family waving from a doorway as a parcel arrives.

example.english: Send us your location on WhatsApp

vocabulary.video_hint: Group arrangements; أرسل لنا / تعال معانا.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Yemeni 'tell someone': خبّرني 'tell me', خبّره 'tell him'. Takes the person straight on the verb. حكى is 'tell a story'; قال لـ 'say to'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man cupping his hand to another man's ear with a speech bubble.

example.english: Tell her the appointment is tomorrow

vocabulary.video_hint: Messages passed between characters; خبّر + suffix.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Sanaa 'give': أدّيني 'give me', أدّاه 'he gave him', أدّيه 'give him'. You will also hear أعطى / عطى and هات 'hand over'. The person comes first, then the thing.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand passing a glass of water into another open hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: Table and shop scenes; أدّيني / هات with the object handed over.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The very Sanaa 'take': شلّه 'take it', شلّيت 'I took', يشلّ. Doubled l. خذ 'take' is understood everywhere.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man lifting a box of vegetables onto his shoulder.

example.english: Take the bag with you home

vocabulary.video_hint: Market and moving scenes; شلّ / خذ as things are picked up.

vocabulary.teaching_note: بعث له 'he sent to him', ابعث لي 'send me'. The person goes on لـ. For messages you will also learn أرسل in Lesson 8.
vocabulary.image_scene: A boy being sent off to the shop with a note, a hand pointing the way.

example.english: Send me your son to carry the qat

vocabulary.teaching_note: ورّيني 'show me', ورّيه 'show him', ورّيتها 'I showed her'. The person on the verb, the thing after. Doubled r.
vocabulary.image_scene: A woman holding up a phone screen to a friend.

example.english: Show me where the house is on the map

vocabulary.video_hint: Anyone showing something on a screen; ورّيني / ورّيكم.

vocabulary.teaching_note: ناديه 'call him', ناديها 'call her'. For a phone call you will learn اتّصل in Lesson 8. صوّت له 'shout for him' is also heard.
vocabulary.image_scene: A mother at a window calling a boy in from the lane.

example.english: Call your brother, lunch is ready

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone summoned from another room; نادي / ناديه.

vocabulary.teaching_note: اسأله 'ask him', سألني 'he asked me', اسألها. The person straight on the verb, the topic with عن.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man with a raised finger asking a shopkeeper, question mark above.

example.arabic: اسأله عن السعر قبل ما تشتري
example.transliteration: isʾaluh ʿan is-siʿr gabl maa tishtari
example.english: Ask him about the price before you buy

vocabulary.teaching_note: جاوبني 'answer me', ما جاوبش 'he didn't answer'. For answering a phone or a message, ردّ is the word (Lesson 8).
vocabulary.image_scene: A student with a raised hand answering, a teacher listening.

example.english: I asked him and he didn't answer me

vocabulary.teaching_note: عنه 'about him', عنها 'about her', عنهم 'about them', عني 'about me'. After اسأل، حكى، كلّم.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two women chatting with a thought bubble showing a third person.

example.english: He told me a lot about you

vocabulary.teaching_note: ساعدني 'help me', ساعده 'help him', ساعدنا 'he helped us'. Person on the verb.
vocabulary.image_scene: A young man helping an old woman carry a water can up steps.

vocabulary.teaching_note: وصّلني 'drop me off', وصّله البيت 'take him home', وصّل الرسالة 'deliver the message'. Doubled ṣ.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man opening a car door for a friend, a house in the distance.

example.english: Drop me at the university, please

vocabulary.video_hint: Taxi and lift scenes; وصّلني + place.

vocabulary.teaching_note: خلّيه 'leave him / let him', خلّيني 'let me', خلّيك 'stay'. Also 'let' before a verb: خلّيه يجي 'let him come'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man raising a hand to stop a friend from following someone.

vocabulary.teaching_note: سلّم لي عليه 'greet him for me' — the sentence that closes every visit. سلّم عليهم 'he greeted them'. The لي is 'on my behalf'.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man raising his hand in greeting to a group across a street.

example.english: Give my greetings to your family

sound_spotlight.example: بيتش، عندش، لش، شفتش (baytish, ʿindish, lish, shuftish)
sound_spotlight.explanation: The Sanaa feminine 'your / you' is a sh. It is the sound that marks a northern speaker; Aden and Taiz say -ik. Note the negative -sh on a verb is a different thing: شفتش can be 'I saw you (f)' — context and stress separate them.
مع grows a long aa before most suffixes but not before -i and -ish: maʿi, maʿish. Hear the length; it carries the word.
Adding endings pushes the stress rightward: khábbar, khabbírni, khabbarnáahum. Yemeni listeners track the ending by where the stress lands.

lesson_sequence.detail: The Um Salem dialogue once; the learner counts how many different people are referred to by endings alone.
One verb (خبّر) and one preposition (لـ) with all eight endings, audio first, then the chart revealed; -ni vs -i highlighted.
The verbs of giving, telling and asking on cards, each with the suffixed imperative as the example.
Audio commands (أدّيه، أدّيها، أدّيهم…); the learner taps the right recipient in a family picture.
The AI gives an instruction about a third person; the learner passes it on with the right ending: قال خبّرها إن…
Ten commands to convert from -ak to -ish, recorded and checked.
Counter; nudge to end the next visit with سلّم لي على…
